items.gist: Śiva is not directly divided; the meaning of sākṣāt is clarified and ekarūpatā is addressed.
The discussion turns to trivedatā, mantramahānātha, and the status of layākala among the tattvas.
The text argues for thirteenfold rather than elevenfold classification, including jñānākala and vedyatā.
Difference is prominent in sakala but not similarly in akalādi; layākala differs only by saṃskāra.
Śiva's svācchandya alone produces difference; the Lord does not state thirteenfold status for layākalādi.
Vedyatā is a property of bhāva; even in inert things consciousness is present, and awakening is discussed.
Awakening is twofold, for mantratva and bhava; different beings awaken differently according to their conditioning.
The avatāra differs in the state of vijñāniyogin; eight vijñānakevalas are mentioned.
Vedyatā is fitness to be known, illustrated by the sleeping beloved and the Lord's creative intention.
The layākala's experience is vivid; memory and bhoktṛtā persist even in deep sleep-like states.
The detailed distinction of tattvas is summarized, with bhedas arising among śakti and śaktimat.
Bhedas and sub-bhedas are countless; even earthly things differ, and full enumeration is not attempted.
The seven mātṛśaktis generate many forms; all is all-pervasive, and subdivision yields endless variety.
Sakala's powers produce further differences; layākalādi also develop differences through saṃskāra and decay.
Different modes of entering, merging, expanding, and revolving produce different vedyatās and bhedas.
The earth tattva and its states are shown; vedyatā is identity with knowers, culminating in Śiva alone.
The earth tattva is displayed; Śivanātha is identified with earth, and mantramaheśvaras direct siddhis.
Those who attain laya at kalpa's end are pralayakevalas; deep sleep shows tattvalīnatva and varied experience.
Memory arises upon subtle awakening; the confused claim of remembered pleasure is rejected.
Earth-dwelling sakalas are bound by karma and impurity; the sevenfold śakti disturbance is stated.
Śiva as acyutacidrūpa has three śaktis; mantras stand threefold, colored by the grasper's form.
